questions.q: Does PostgreSQL core have a built-in Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) feature, per this lesson?
options: Yes — it is enabled with CREATE EXTENSION tde
No — PostgreSQL core has no TDE equivalent to Oracle's or SQL Server's
PostgreSQL has TDE but only for tables using pgcrypto
Yes — it is enabled by default on every new database
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that PostgreSQL core has no built-in TDE equivalent, unlike Oracle and SQL Server.

questions.q: How is SSL/TLS enforced for PostgreSQL connections, per this lesson?
options: Using the hostssl connection type in pg_hba.conf, requiring SSL for matching connections
Only through a third-party proxy sitting in front of PostgreSQL
SSL/TLS cannot be enforced in PostgreSQL at all
By setting a single global flag in postgresql.conf with no per-connection control
questions.explain: pg_hba.conf's hostssl connection type (in place of host) requires SSL for connections matching that rule, giving fine-grained enforcement.

questions.q: What is pgcrypto used for, per this lesson?
options: Enforcing SSL/TLS on client connections
Managing pg_hba.conf authentication rules
Column-level encryption of specific sensitive fields, plus hashing functions like crypt() and digest()
Whole-database transparent encryption at rest, replacing the need for TDE
questions.explain: pgcrypto is described as the real extension for encrypting specific column values, along with hashing functions commonly used for password storage.

questions.q: What is the real, common approach PostgreSQL deployments use for whole-database at-rest encryption, per this lesson?
options: There is no way to achieve at-rest encryption with PostgreSQL under any approach
Relying on SSL/TLS, which also encrypts data at rest
Encrypting every column individually with pgcrypto, one at a time
Filesystem-level or full-disk encryption, such as LUKS, BitLocker, or cloud storage-level encryption
questions.explain: The lesson identifies filesystem or full-disk encryption as the real, common way PostgreSQL deployments achieve whole-database at-rest encryption, transparent to PostgreSQL itself.

questions.q: Who is responsible for key management when using pgcrypto, per this lesson?
options: PostgreSQL manages all keys automatically with no DBA involvement
The DBA or application — pgcrypto does not manage keys automatically
pgAudit manages encryption keys on pgcrypto's behalf
Key management is handled entirely by pg_hba.conf
questions.explain: The lesson notes that key management is the DBA's or application's responsibility with pgcrypto, unlike platforms with integrated key management built into TDE.
